Recommending Controls: Processes, Procedures, and Policies That Mitigate Risk

Unit 3: Risk, Recalls, and Data Security. Lesson 15 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

An investigation closes and the recommendation writes itself: retrain the staff. Six months later the same event happens on a different unit. Retraining is the weakest control available, and a manager who reaches for it first will spend a career fixing the same thing. This lesson is about choosing a control that holds and proving that it did.

The hierarchy of controls, applied to healthcare technology

Strongest first. Work down the list only when the one above it is genuinely impossible.

Control            What it means here                   Example
Eliminate          remove the hazard entirely           retire the model that has
                                                        no free-flow protection
Substitute         replace it with something safer      standardize on one pump
                                                        with a drug library
Engineer           design the hazard out so a person    hard dose limits, interlocks,
                   cannot reach it                      keyed connectors, segmented
                                                        network, tamper-proof settings
Administer         change what people are told to do    a procedure, a policy, a
                                                        checklist, a second signature,
                                                        a maintenance interval
Protect            put equipment between the person     gloves, eye protection,
                   and the hazard                       lockout devices

Engineering controls work whether or not anyone is paying attention; administrative controls work only while attention lasts. That is why a device configuration change usually beats a memo, and why the committee should hear both options with their cost.

Writing a procedure or policy that actually controls the risk

A policy says what the organization requires and who is accountable. A procedure says who does what, in what order, with what, and what the record is. A control written as prose nobody can follow is not a control.

  1. State the risk the document exists to control, in one sentence.
  2. Name the trigger: what starts the procedure.
  3. Number the steps in the order a person performs them, one action per step.
  4. Name the roles, not the people, so it survives a resignation.
  5. Say what record is made, where it is kept, and for how long.
  6. Say what to do when a step cannot be completed, and who to escalate to.
  7. Date it, version it, name the owner, and set a review date.

Reference the organization's other policies rather than repeating them, so one change does not leave three documents disagreeing.

Training and competency as controls

Training is a legitimate control when the gap really is knowledge and when it is backed by competency assessment rather than an attendance sheet. Competency means the person demonstrated the task, was observed, and the observation was recorded. For operators, take in-service education to the pattern you measured, on every shift that touches the device, and record who was trained on what, by whom, and when. For staff, documented assessment per person and per equipment type. Training with no assessment behind it is a note in a file, and a surveyor will read it as one.

Measuring whether a control works

Decide the measure before you implement the control, and take a baseline. Then measure the same thing the same way: the event count or near-miss count, the use error code frequency on that model and unit, repeat repairs, overdue scheduled maintenance, audit results on the new procedure's records, and the completion of the training. Set a date to report. A control with no measure attached cannot be defended and cannot be withdrawn, so the department accumulates procedures forever and knows nothing about any of them.

Presenting the recommendation to the committee that owns it

Match the control to the committee. Device-related events and use error trends go to patient safety. Equipment inventory, completion rates, recalls, and the annual plan evaluation go to the environment of care committee. Investigations, device holds, and reportable events go to risk management. Metrics with targets and corrective action results go to performance improvement. Imaging and therapy equipment performance goes to radiation safety, device cleaning and disinfection to infection control. Whichever it is, bring one page: the risk, the options with cost, your recommendation, the measure you will report, and the decision you need from them.

Exam tip: work the hierarchy from the top. Eliminate, substitute, and engineer beat administrative controls and personal protective equipment, and retraining alone is the weakest answer on any list. Define the measure and the baseline before you implement, and take the recommendation to the committee that owns that risk.
Remember
Controls are chosen from the top of the hierarchy down, written as a procedure with roles, records, and a review date, measured against a baseline set before implementation, and taken to the committee that owns the risk.
Deeper explanation

Recommending Controls: Processes, Procedures, and Policies That Mitigate Risk, explained slowly

A control decision, worked down the hierarchy

A pump fleet has produced three wrong-concentration events in a year. Here is the same risk addressed at five different levels, with what each costs and how long it lasts.

Level        Control                          Cost        How long it holds
Eliminate    retire the two models without    $380,000    permanently; the
             a drug library                   capital     hazard is gone
Substitute   standardize the whole fleet on   $140,000    permanently for the
             the model that has hard limits   capital     devices replaced
Engineer     configure hard concentration     $0 to        indefinitely; it
             limits in the library on every   $9,000       works whether or not
             pump that supports them          of labor     anyone is watching
Administer   a policy requiring a second-     staff time   as long as staffing,
             person check, plus a procedure   only         attention, and
             and an audit                                  turnover allow
Protect      nothing applicable; personal     n/a          n/a
             protective equipment does not
             address a dosing error

The recommendation here is the engineering control first, because it costs almost nothing and does not depend on attention, with the substitution carried into the capital plan and the administrative control used only on the devices that cannot take a hard limit. Bring all of it to the committee. A committee shown one option has been handed a decision, not asked for one.

A procedure that controls a risk, in full

TITLE        Securing a device involved in a patient event
PURPOSE      To preserve the device and its evidence so the hospital can
             determine cause and meet its reporting obligations.
OWNER        HTM manager        VERSION 3      REVIEW BY  next March
TRIGGER      Any report that a patient was or may have been harmed while a
             medical device was in use.

STEPS
1  The clinical staff remove the device from patient use immediately and
   do not clean, adjust, reset, or power it off.
2  The charge nurse calls HTM and the risk manager. HTM responds on site.
3  HTM photographs the device, screen, controls, and connections as found.
4  HTM collects the accessories, cables, sensors, and disposables in use,
   including packaging and the contents of the room's trash.
5  HTM pulls event and error logs by the manufacturer's documented method
   and records who pulled them and when.
6  HTM tags the device OUT OF SERVICE, moves it to the secured location,
   and records the chain of custody.
7  HTM supplies the device identification to the risk manager within one
   hour: manufacturer, model, serial, software version, lot numbers.
8  No repair, calibration, update, or return to service occurs until the
   risk manager releases the device in writing.

IF A STEP CANNOT BE COMPLETED
   Record what could not be done and why, and notify the risk manager
   immediately. Escalate to the HTM manager and the administrator on call.

RECORD       The event file: photographs, logs, custody record, device
             identification, and the release. Retained per the hospital's
             retention schedule.

Read what makes it a control rather than an essay: a trigger, numbered single actions, roles rather than names, a record, an exception path, and a review date.

Measuring a control

Control                        Measure                    Baseline  Target  When
Hard concentration limits      wrong-concentration             3/yr     0    quarterly
in the drug library            events
Second-person check policy     audit compliance on 20            n/a    90%  monthly
                               observed programmings                          for 6
                                                                              months
In-service on every shift      use error codes on this          17/qtr   <5   quarterly
                               model
New securing procedure         event files complete on           40%    100%  per event
                               audit
Competency assessment          staff assessed competent          4 of    8 of  annual
on the new fleet                                                  8       8

Set the baseline before you implement, or you will spend a year arguing about whether anything improved.

Matching the control to its committee

What you are bringing                        Committee
device-related events, near misses, use      patient safety
error trends, alarm issues
equipment inventory, completion rates,       environment of care
recalls, the annual plan evaluation,
utility and construction impacts
investigation reports, device holds,         risk management
reportable events
metrics with targets and trends, the         performance improvement
results of corrective actions
imaging and therapy equipment                radiation safety
performance, survey results
cleaning and disinfection, water systems,    infection control
sterilizers, loaner handling

What to memorize

Hierarchy         eliminate, substitute, engineer, administer, protect
Rule of thumb     engineering controls hold without attention; administrative
                  controls hold only while attention lasts
Retraining alone  the weakest answer on any list
Procedure         risk, trigger, numbered steps, roles, record, exception
                  path, owner, version, review date
Competency        demonstrated, observed, recorded; attendance is not
                  competency
Measurement       defined with a baseline before implementation
